title: Round 10: Final senior-level system design with interviewer follow-ups
description: Combine everything from the previous rounds into a senior-level system design interview, and learn how to handle follow-up questions about scale, cost, and trade-offs.

data.text: In the final round, the interviewer expects you to lead the conversation. You will clarify requirements, propose a design, and then respond to follow-ups about scaling, cost, availability, and operational complexity. The difference between a mid-level and a senior answer is not the number of components you draw; it is how you reason about trade-offs under changing constraints.
What senior means in system design

items: You ask clarifying questions before drawing a single box.
You estimate scale back-of-the-envelope style and validate those numbers with the interviewer.
You identify single points of failure and describe how you would eliminate them.
You discuss cost and team readiness, not just technical elegance.
You admit what you do not know and explain how you would find out.

terms.definition: A distributed system can simultaneously provide only two of three guarantees: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
Rough calculations using round numbers to validate whether a design can handle expected scale.
A component whose failure would bring down the entire system.
A target value or range for a service level, such as 99.9% availability or 200ms p99 latency.
Reducing cloud spend without breaking SLAs through reserved instances, spot instances, and tiered storage.

data.text: Start every system design by restating the problem in your own words. 'If I understand correctly, we need a system that lets users upload photos, applies AI tags, and serves resized images to web and mobile clients. We expect ten million uploads per month and want sub-second page loads.' That restatement gives the interviewer a chance to correct you and shows that you listen.

data.title: Handling a follow-up
data.content: Example of a senior response to a scaling follow-up:
data.code:
Interviewer: 'What if traffic triples next quarter?'

Senior answer:
1. Identify the bottlenecks: image processing and database writes.
2. Propose a queue between upload and processing to absorb bursts.
3. Move processed images to object storage with a CDN in front.
4. Partition the database by user ID so writes scale horizontally.
5. Estimate the cost of the added queue and storage and compare it to the cost of a multi-hour outage.

items: Consistency versus availability: when is it acceptable to serve stale data?
Cost optimization: how do you reduce cloud spend without breaking SLAs?
Observability: what metrics, logs, and traces would you add before launch?
Team structure: how does the architecture map to engineering teams and on-call rotations?
Migration: how do you move from the current system to the new design without downtime?
Define SLOs before launch: availability target, latency target, and error budget.
Build a dashboard with golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
Write runbooks for the top three failure modes so on-call engineers know how to respond.
Test the system with chaos engineering: kill a node, throttle the database, and observe recovery.
Plan the launch ceremony: feature flags, canary percentages, and a rollback trigger.
Estimate costs: compute, storage, network egress, and third-party services. Show the interviewer you can build within a budget.

data.caption: Senior system design flow from requirements to launch
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Clarify requirements] --> B[Estimate scale: users, QPS, storage]
    B --> C[Identify constraints: latency, consistency, compliance]
    C --> D[High-level design: components and data flow]
    D --> E[Deep dive: database schema, APIs, caching]
    E --> F[Identify single points of failure]
    F --> G[Add redundancy and failover]
    G --> H[Define SLOs and SLIs]
    H --> I[Design observability: metrics, logs, traces]
    I --> J[Plan migration and launch]
    J --> K[Review cost and team readiness]
    K --> L[Deliver design with trade-offs documented]

cards.title: Strong consistency
cards.description: All nodes see the same data at the same time.

cards.title: Eventual consistency
cards.description: Data propagates to all nodes eventually; temporary inconsistencies are allowed.

cards.title: Causal consistency
cards.description: Guarantees that causally related operations are seen in order.
cons: Harder to reason about than strong consistency

data.title: Clarify before you design
data.text: If the interviewer gives you a vague requirement, ask for numbers. 'How many daily active users?' 'What is the maximum acceptable latency?' 'Do we need audit logs?' Numbers unlock better design decisions and show that you think in terms of measurable outcomes.

items: Use reserved instances for baseline compute; spot instances for batch workers.
Tier storage: hot data in SSD, warm in standard object storage, cold in archive.
Cache aggressively at the edge: CDN for static assets, Redis for hot database queries.
Right-size instances: use smaller instances with autoscaling instead of a few large ones.
Compress data in transit and at rest to reduce egress costs.
Set budget alerts and review cost attribution tags weekly.

items.question: How do I handle a follow-up about cost?
items.answer: Break down the major cost drivers: compute, storage, network egress, and third-party services. Propose a tiered architecture where cheap, scalable resources serve the majority of traffic and expensive resources handle only edge cases.

items.question: What if the interviewer asks for a technology I do not know well?
items.answer: Be honest about your familiarity, then reason from first principles. 'I have not used this database in production, but based on its consistency model and throughput claims, I would evaluate it for this workload by...'

items.question: How detailed should my data model be?
items.answer: Draw enough tables or document stores to show you understand the relationships and access patterns. You do not need every column, but you should know which fields are indexed and which queries are hot.

items.question: What if I realize my design has a flaw mid-way?
items.answer: Say so explicitly. 'I initially thought we could use a single database, but given the write volume, I would shard by user ID and use a separate analytics store for reporting.' Self-correction is a senior signal.

data.title: Design a URL shortening service
data.description: Complete a full system design for a URL shortening service like bit.ly. Include requirements clarification, capacity estimation, API design, data model, and follow-up handling for scale and cost.
steps: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements with the interviewer
Estimate QPS and storage for 100 million URLs per year
Design the write path: shorten API, database schema, and cache strategy
Design the read path: redirect handler, CDN, and cache invalidation
Discuss follow-ups: analytics, custom aliases, spam prevention, and cost
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a design that addresses scale, latency, cost, and operational concerns, and you should be able to discuss trade-offs when the interviewer changes the constraints.

data.title: Summary
points: Restate the problem and ask for scale and latency requirements
Design for the most critical path first, then discuss edge cases
Address follow-ups with trade-offs, not one-size-fits-all answers
Connect the architecture to cost, team structure, and operational reality
data.takeaway: A senior system design answer is a conversation. You guide the interviewer through requirements, trade-offs, and risk, and you leave them confident that you can ship the system you described.
